codex.worst_flaw: The pilot is not launchable as written because technicians can forfeit reward credit by placing a hazardous job on hold immediately, creating an incentive to delay the safety stop.

claude.worst_flaw: The design doesn't say how to check checklist quality beyond a 10-record weekly sample, and it never checks for displacement. For example, a technician could tick every box without inspecting anything, or an at-risk job could be recorded as 'attended' late. The pause trigger is also too coarse to catch either at a 300-person scale.

holistic.reason: It is a well-designed, union-co-developed pilot that rewards completion without penalising hazard stops, removes friction, and has staggered measurement and pressure safeguards, though the one-hour-off reward is modest and the 75% threshold plus admin load may limit salience and durability.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-defect pause rule allows rewards to continue after a confirmed failure to escalate a hazard, making the pilot unsafe to launch as written.

claude.worst_flaw: Operability and learning are thin: no replayable event or policy versioning, no independent shadow validation, a single coordinator as the only appeal route, and only a 2-week comparison between the two crew groups, with no plan for spillovers between crews, sample size or uncertainty.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, private non-punitive tracking, workflow fixes first, a stepped-wedge pilot with a clear keep/change/drop rule and weekly audits against gaming make it approvable, but a 30-minute release reward may feel modest and gains may fade once rewards stop, even with the checklist default in place.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says how pre-start checks will be checked against what is actually on site. The weekly sample of 10 credited jobs is matched only against existing records, so a pencil-whipped checklist that is complete and on time would pass, and the crew stagger compares only two weeks with no stated sample size, uncertainty handling or cost and harm criteria.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the audit can detect technicians earning rewards by submitting complete-looking checklists while skipping the underlying safety checks.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, private feedback, a modest reward, safeguards against backfilling and pressure, and a staggered rollout with a clear decision metric make this approvable. Noticing depends on a 30-minute reward and a weekly briefing, and lasting change depends on the workflow fix of making the checklist the first action in the job.

claude.worst_flaw: The staggered two-group comparison runs over only two weeks with about 25 engineers, so it cannot separate reward effects from noise or from spillover between groups that share backup reviewers. The design also lacks replayable rule versions, shadow validation of the counting rule against hand-checked cases, and a staffed appeal path beyond the maintainer fixing counts.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-week comparison between ownership groups lacks a rule for separating the reward’s effect from differences in baseline performance, PR mix, and cross-group backup coverage.

holistic.reason: The design is unusually careful (private feedback, no leaderboards, team-level reward, a clear counting rule, a staggered comparison and pre-set thresholds), but it is complex for a sceptical 25-person team, the reward is a modest learning block, and the 45-minute weekly overhead and sampling rules could feel heavy. The lasting effect will depend mostly on whether the queue and backup routing become real habits.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-week stagger leaves the lunch’s effect confounded with differences in review complexity, reviewer capacity, and work shared across rotations.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design only compares two rotations over a two-week stagger, with no predefined uncertainty, spillover handling or harm and cost thresholds, and the personal 4-of-5 goal does not account for uneven PR complexity or reviewers who pick up few reviews.

holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck (routing and protected review time) before rewarding, uses a team-level metric with private feedback and a sceptic-friendly small reward, and has solid gaming guards, but it is complex to explain, adds weekly sampling overhead and relies on the lunch motivating a sceptical team.

claude.worst_flaw: The 80% group target has no tie to the recalculated baseline, and it ignores PR size, reviewer load and uneven volume across groups. The two-group stagger, with only about 25 engineers, also leaves too few groups to separate the effect of the lunch from the shared workflow changes and time trends.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The code host records review timing and disposition, but the design relies on five weekly spot checks to validate whether the reviews driving the reported success rate and lunch eligibility were useful.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot: fixes friction first, targets reviewer response with quality guards, private individual feedback and team-level lunch reward suits sceptical engineers, with a clear exit rule and a plan to make the workflow the default. It is a bit heavy on rules and measurement, so engagement may be modest, but the process changes (queue, rotation, protected time) should persist after the lunches end.

codex.worst_flaw: The meal depends on matching observed actions to kiosk entries, but the design sets no acceptable false-match rate and specifies no independent shadow test to show that unrelated entries cannot routinely earn credit.

claude.worst_flaw: The design rewards logging fidelity, not correct hand hygiene. Its only compliance guardrail is a 5-point drop that triggers a pause, so logging could improve while hygiene quality slides below that threshold. It also has weak event-history, versioning and appeal staffing, and its three-ward stepped design uses only about 20 assessable actions per ward, which cannot separate the incentive effect from noise or month-to-month case mix.

holistic.reason: Unusually careful design that rewards accurate logging, audits against observers, protects care priority and pauses on drift, but the monthly team meal is a weak, delayed prompt and its heavy measurement and rollout complexity may blunt engagement and retention once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout rule can make the kiosk the default based on one usable entry per staffed shift block even if most eligible moments go unlogged and audited hand-hygiene compliance declines.

claude.worst_flaw: Learning compares only three wards with staggered starts, has no plain-support control beyond one month and no preset outcome, harm or cost decision for the reward itself, and the kiosk-uptake rollout thresholds cannot show whether logging is complete or accurate.

holistic.reason: Well-designed: rewards audited behaviour rather than self-reports, avoids surveillance, has safeguards and a staggered rollout, but the collective ward-level catered-break reward is modest and diffuse, and the kiosk's lasting adoption depends on workflow fit once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never defines the target behaviour for the kiosk itself. The reward depends on observed audit compliance, but the success and exit criteria use kiosk log rate per bed-day, so the two measures are not reconciled. Logging rate is also not normalised against real hand-hygiene opportunities. Event history, policy versioning and a staffed appeal process are thin or missing.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait for a valid adoption measure because logs per occupied bed-day can rise even as nurses log a smaller share of eligible hand-hygiene moments, yet that rate drives the decision to keep the kiosk as the default.

holistic.reason: Rewarding ward-level audited hygiene with logging as a zero-point adoption metric, plus staged rollout, safeguards and a quality stop, is sound and approvable, but a four-week meal reward and a kiosk-log-rate durability test make awareness modest and lasting habit uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The staggered rollout does not reliably isolate the effect of paid flex time from differences between cohorts, spillover between teams, and changes to the resolution workflow.

claude.worst_flaw: The design applies one flat 30% target to every agent and adds no case-mix or small-book handling. Agents in queues where articles rarely fit, or with very few eligible tickets, get unfair or noisy results. The keep/change/drop decision also uses absolute post-programme rates, so it cannot tell the reward's added value apart from the workflow fixes or seasonal case mix, even with a two-week cohort stagger.

holistic.reason: Workflow-first design, verifiable counting, anti-gaming sampling, a pre-set keep/change/drop rule and a clean end make this approvable, but 30 minutes of flex time for a four-week window is a modest reward and the private feedback may not be salient enough to drive attention, and lasting effect depends on the embedded workflow fixes.

codex.worst_flaw: Agents can shrink the denominator used for rewards and pilot evaluation by marking tickets as inapplicable, and the design specifies neither a testable applicability rule nor a pause threshold for misclassified exclusions.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never reconciles the article-link goal with the CSAT bonus or customer outcomes. Its decision metric is coverage corrected by a 10-ticket weekly sample, so a 40% target can be met with marginally useful links. It also has no appeal path and no event or policy versioning for disputed counts.

holistic.reason: Workflow-first, quality sampling, CSAT guardrails and a staggered rollout are strong and well-controlled, but the reward is modest (30 minutes of paid time), the programme is complex for a 60-person org, and the lasting effect depends mostly on the default workflow change rather than on motivation.

codex.worst_flaw: The 50% threshold counts tickets with no safe, relevant article opportunity against teams, so differences in ticket mix can drive both payouts and the rollout decision.

claude.worst_flaw: The personal goal is a flat 50% of each agent's resolved tickets, with no baseline, case-mix or ticket-type adjustment. Small books and agents with many tickets that have no safe article are not handled, and with only a few teams per wave the randomized comparison is underpowered and has no stated sample-size or uncertainty plan.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with quality checks, pilot-style comparison, and fix-the-workflow-first approach, but the one-paid-hour team reward is modest, the multi-step rules are complex for agents to absorb, and sustained behaviour depends on the workflow fixes since the incentive expires after four weeks.
